items.title: The Satavahanas in Andhra — the Eastern Dimension
items.body:
## The Satavahanas as the 'Andhras'

**In one line:** This note looks only at the Andhra (eastern) side of the Satavahanas — the part that makes them the opening chapter of Andhra Pradesh's own history.

**The story**
The pan-India Satavahana story (Simuka, Gautamiputra Satakarni, the Nasik Prashasti) is told under Ancient India. Here the focus is Andhra. The **Puranas call these rulers the 'Andhras'**, and their long rule (c. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE) grew the roots of Andhra's classical culture. While **Pratishthana (Paithan)** on the Godavari was the western capital, the **eastern power-centre** was **Dhanyakataka** — with the fortified town of **Dharanikota**, right next to **Amaravati** on the Krishna. The fertile lower Krishna–Godavari delta was the richest part of the realm and a hub of **maritime trade**: Andhra cotton and muslin were prized as far away as Rome. The court also nurtured **Prakrit literature** (Hala's Gatha Saptasati, Gunadhya's Brihatkatha) and, above all, made Andhra the **cradle of Indian Buddhist art** at Amaravati.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC treats the Satavahanas as Band-A AP history; the Puranic name 'Andhras' and the eastern capital Dhanyakataka are direct, repeat facts.

**Picture it**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Puranic name | Andhras / Andhra-bhrityas |
| Western capital | Pratishthana (Paithan), on the Godavari |
| Eastern centre | Dhanyakataka / Dharanikota (near Amaravati) |
| Economy | Krishna–Godavari delta; Roman textile trade |
| Culture | Prakrit literature; Amaravati Buddhist art |

**Terms explained**
- **Dhanyakataka** — the eastern Satavahana capital on the Krishna, beside Amaravati.
- **Dharanikota** — the fortified township attached to Dhanyakataka.
- **Andhra-bhrityas** — 'Andhra servants', another Puranic label for the dynasty.

**Don't confuse**
- **Dhanyakataka** (eastern capital) is NOT the same as **Pratishthana/Paithan** (western capital) — two ends of one empire.
- The **Andhras** of the Puranas = the Satavahana dynasty, NOT the modern linguistic state.

**Remember it:** 'Andhras of the Puranas — Paithan in the west, Dhanyakataka (by Amaravati) in the east'.

**TL;DR**
- The Puranas call the Satavahanas the 'Andhras'.
- Western capital Pratishthana (Paithan); eastern centre Dhanyakataka/Dharanikota near Amaravati.
- Krishna–Godavari delta drove Roman textile trade.
- Court Prakrit literature; cradle of the Amaravati art school.
keyPoints: The Puranas call the Satavahanas the 'Andhras'.
Western capital = Pratishthana (Paithan); eastern centre = Dhanyakataka/Dharanikota near Amaravati.
Krishna-Godavari delta drove maritime trade, exporting textiles to Rome.
Court Prakrit literature: Hala's Gatha Saptasati and Gunadhya's Brihatkatha (Paisachi).
Satavahana era = cradle of the Amaravati school of Buddhist art.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi); Wikipedia — Satavahana dynasty (verified)

items.title: Amaravati Stupa & the Amaravati School of Art
items.body:
## The Mahachaitya and its art school

**In one line:** The Amaravati Stupa is Andhra's greatest ancient monument, and the sculpture style it created — the Amaravati school — ranks with Gandhara and Mathura as one of India's three great early schools.

**The story**
On the Krishna at **Amaravati (Palnadu district)** stands the **Mahachaitya**, a huge Buddhist stupa built and enlarged in phases between about the **3rd century BCE and c. 250 CE** under the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus. Its Andhra signature is clear: a hemispherical **anda (dome)**, a great carved **railing**, and sets of **five ayaka pillars** standing on platforms at each of the four sides. Over time its carvers developed a style all their own — **crowded, flowing narrative panels** of Jataka stories and the Buddha's life, cut in the region's **white-greenish limestone**. This became the **Amaravati school of art**, and it travelled: it shaped Buddhist sculpture in **Sri Lanka and South-East Asia**. The site is protected by the **ASI**, though many of its finest marbles now sit in the **Government Museum, Chennai** and the **British Museum** (the 'Amaravati Marbles'), carried off after Colin Mackenzie's surveys.

**Why it is asked**
Telling the three schools apart (material + region) and placing Amaravati in Palnadu are classic discrimination and match questions.

**Picture it**

| School | Material | Region |
|---|---|---|
| Gandhara | grey schist | North-West frontier |
| Mathura | red sandstone | Uttar Pradesh |
| Amaravati | white limestone | Krishna valley, Andhra |

**Terms explained**
- **Mahachaitya** — a great stupa / Buddhist shrine.
- **Anda** — the hemispherical dome of a stupa.
- **Ayaka pillars** — groups of five pillars on a platform, unique to Andhra stupas.
- **Aniconic** — showing the Buddha by symbols (empty throne, footprints) rather than a human figure.

**Don't confuse**
- **Amaravati** = white limestone; **Gandhara** = grey schist (Greco-Roman look); **Mathura** = red sandstone. Do not swap the materials.
- The 'Amaravati Marbles' in London are the ORIGINAL carvings removed in colonial times, NOT copies.

**Remember it:** 'Three schools by stone — G-schist, M-sandstone, A-limestone' (Gandhara, Mathura, Amaravati).

**TL;DR**
- Amaravati Mahachaitya (Palnadu) built in phases c. 3rd c BCE–250 CE; ASI-protected.
- Andhra stupa signature = five ayaka pillars on each of the four sides.
- One of three great early schools, with Gandhara and Mathura.
- White-limestone narrative reliefs; influenced Sri Lanka and South-East Asia; marbles now in Chennai and the British Museum.
keyPoints: Amaravati Mahachaitya (Palnadu dist.) built in phases c.3rd c BCE-250 CE, ASI-protected.
Andhra stupa signature = five ayaka pillars on each of the four sides.
Amaravati is one of three great early schools with Gandhara and Mathura.
Medium = white-greenish limestone; style = crowded narrative Jataka reliefs.
Amaravati art influenced Sri Lanka and South-East Asia; marbles now in Chennai and the British Museum.
items.mnemonic: Three schools by stone = 'G-schist, M-sandstone, A-limestone' (Gandhara, Mathura, Amaravati).

items.title: The Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)
items.body:
## Successors of the Satavahanas

**In one line:** The Ikshvakus were the first dynasty to rule the eastern Krishna valley after the Satavahanas, famous for a court where the kings were Hindu but the queens funded Buddhism.

**The story**
When the Satavahana empire broke up, the **Andhra Ikshvakus** took over the **eastern Krishna valley** and ruled for a little over a century in the **3rd–4th centuries CE**. Their capital was **Vijayapuri**, in the **Nagarjunakonda** valley. Historians call them the *Andhra Ikshvakus* to keep them apart from the legendary solar-dynasty Ikshvakus of Kosala (Rama's line). Their kings came in the order **Vasishthiputra Chamtamula (founder) → Virapurushadatta → Ehuvala Chamtamula → Rudrapurushadatta (last)**, and they kept the Satavahana habit of **matronymic** names. The most striking feature of their court was a **religious division within the royal household**: the **kings stayed Brahmanical**, performing Vedic rites (agnihotra, vajapeya, ashvamedha), while the **royal women** — above all the princess **Chamtisiri** — were **generous Buddhist donors** who paid for the Mahachaitya and monasteries at Nagarjunakonda.

**Why it is asked**
'Capital of the Andhra Ikshvakus = Vijayapuri', the founder's name, and the kings-Vedic / women-Buddhist contrast are all repeat APPSC points.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Region / period | Eastern Krishna valley, 3rd–4th c CE |
| Capital | Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda) |
| Founder | Vasishthiputra Chamtamula |
| Succession | Chamtamula → Virapurushadatta → Ehuvala Chamtamula → Rudrapurushadatta |
| Religion | Kings Vedic; royal women (Chamtisiri) Buddhist |

**Terms explained**
- **Vijayapuri** — the Ikshvaku capital, in the Nagarjunakonda valley on the Krishna.
- **Matronymic** — a name formed from the mother's name (e.g. Vasishthiputra = 'son of Vasishthi').
- **Vajapeya / agnihotra** — Vedic sacrifices the kings performed to show royal status.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Andhra Ikshvakus** (a real Krishna-valley dynasty) are NOT the legendary **Ikshvakus of Kosala** (Rama's solar line).
- Among the Ikshvakus the **kings were Hindu**; it was the **women** who were Buddhist patrons — not the reverse.

**Remember it:** 'Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri — Vedic kings, Buddhist queens; founder Chamtamula'.

**TL;DR**
- Ikshvakus ruled the eastern Krishna valley (3rd–4th c CE) from Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda).
- Called Andhra Ikshvakus, distinct from the Ikshvakus of Kosala.
- Order: Chamtamula (founder) → Virapurushadatta → Ehuvala Chamtamula → Rudrapurushadatta.
- Kings performed Vedic sacrifices; royal women (Chamtisiri) were the Buddhist patrons.
keyPoints: Ikshvakus ruled the eastern Krishna valley (3rd-4th c CE) from Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda).
Called Andhra Ikshvakus to distinguish them from the Ikshvakus of Kosala.
Ruler order: Chamtamula (founder) -> Virapurushadatta -> Ehuvala Chamtamula -> Rudrapurushadatta.
Kings performed Vedic sacrifices (ashvamedha); they retained matronymics.
Royal women (e.g. Chamtisiri) were the great Buddhist patrons of Nagarjunakonda.

items.title: Nagarjunakonda, Acharya Nagarjuna & Andhra Buddhism
items.body:
## A great Buddhist campus and its philosopher

**In one line:** Nagarjunakonda was a huge Buddhist university-town named after Acharya Nagarjuna, the philosopher who founded the Madhyamika school — and it was rescued from a dam reservoir and rebuilt as an island museum.

**The story**
The valley takes its name from **Acharya Nagarjuna** and held a dense campus of **mahachaityas (great stupas), viharas (monasteries) and study-halls**, plus a rare **stadium/amphitheatre**. Excavations even uncovered a **monastery for monks from Sri Lanka**, showing that Andhra was a launch-pad for Buddhism's journey to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. In the 20th century the **Nagarjuna Sagar dam** reservoir **submerged** the valley, so archaeologists **excavated the relics and re-erected them on a hilltop that is now an island museum**. The man behind the name, **Nagarjuna**, founded the **Madhyamika** (middle-path) school and its doctrine of **Sunyavada** ('emptiness'), writing the **Mula-madhyamaka-karika**; tradition links him to **Sriparvata** (the Nagarjunakonda–Srisailam hills), and his dialectic shaped later thought, including Sankara's Advaita. Andhra more widely was a Buddhist heartland: the **Buddha is traditionally said to have preached the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka**, the **Mahasanghika-derived Chaitika (Andhaka) schools** were strong in the Krishna valley, and the **cult of Avalokitesvara** is believed to have begun here. Buddhism flourished over a millennium and declined from about the **6th century CE**.

**Why it is asked**
Nagarjuna = Madhyamika/Sunyavada, Vijayapuri = Nagarjunakonda, and the submerged-site-to-island-museum story are high-frequency facts.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Site | Nagarjunakonda (= Vijayapuri), Krishna valley |
| Features | Mahachaityas, viharas, Sri Lankan monks' monastery, amphitheatre |
| Rescue | Submerged by Nagarjuna Sagar dam → island museum |
| Nagarjuna | Madhyamika school; Sunyavada; Mula-madhyamaka-karika |
| Wider Andhra | Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka; Chaitika/Andhaka schools; Avalokitesvara cult |

**Terms explained**
- **Madhyamika** — the 'middle path' school of Mahayana Buddhist philosophy.
- **Sunyavada** — the doctrine that all things are 'empty' of fixed independent essence.
- **Vihara** — a Buddhist monastery; **Mahachaitya** — a great stupa.
- **Mahasanghika / Chaitika (Andhaka)** — early Buddhist sub-schools strong in the Krishna valley.

**Don't confuse**
- **Acharya Nagarjuna** the philosopher is different from the modern **Nagarjuna Sagar dam** — the dam is named after the place, which is named after him.
- Nagarjuna founded **Madhyamika (Sunyavada)**, NOT Yogachara (that is Asanga/Vasubandhu).

**Remember it:** 'Nagarjunakonda = Vijayapuri; Nagarjuna = emptiness (Sunyavada); dam drowned it, so it became an island museum'.

**TL;DR**
- Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri) had mahachaityas, viharas and a monastery for Sri Lankan monks.
- Submerged by the Nagarjuna Sagar dam; monuments moved to an island museum.
- Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school (Sunyavada); wrote the Mula-madhyamaka-karika.
- Andhra was a Buddhist heartland (Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka; Chaitika schools; Avalokitesvara cult); decline from c. 6th c CE.
keyPoints: Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri) had mahachaityas, viharas and a monastery for Sri Lankan monks.
Its monuments were submerged by the Nagarjuna Sagar dam and moved to an island museum.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school (Sunyavada); wrote the Mula-madhyamaka-karika.
Buddha traditionally preached the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka.
Andhaka/Chaitika (Mahasanghika) schools and the Avalokitesvara cult are linked to Andhra; decline from c.6th c CE.
items.source: Wikipedia — Nagarjunakonda / Nagarjuna; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: Buddhist Sites of Andhra — a Map
items.body:
## Andhra's Buddhist geography

**In one line:** Coastal Andhra holds one of India's densest clusters of ancient Buddhist sites, and the exam tests which site sits where and why each matters.

**The story**
From the Satavahana age onward, the Krishna–Godavari coast filled with stupas and monasteries covering all three phases of Buddhism — **Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana**. Two sites carry special weight. **Bhattiprolu** (Bapatla/Guntur) yielded inscribed **Buddha relic caskets** whose letters are **one of the earliest specimens of Brahmi in South India** — the **Bhattiprolu script**, regarded as an ancestor of the **Telugu–Kannada** script family. **Salihundam**, on the south bank of the **Vamsadhara** near Kalingapatnam in **Srikakulam**, shows the full **Hinayana → Mahayana → Vajrayana** evolution in the Kalinga borderland. Around these cluster many more: the Krishna-valley core (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli) and the Visakhapatnam hill-monasteries (Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram).

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-column questions (site → district/river/feature) are a staple; Bhattiprolu (script) and Salihundam (Vamsadhara, three phases) are the usual hinges.

**Picture it**

| Site | Location | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Amaravati | Palnadu (Krishna) | Mahachaitya; Amaravati art school |
| Nagarjunakonda | Palnadu (Krishna) | Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri |
| Bhattiprolu | Bapatla/Guntur | relic caskets; Bhattiprolu Brahmi script |
| Salihundam | Srikakulam (Vamsadhara) | Kalinga site; all three phases |
| Guntupalli | West Godavari | early rock-cut chaitya (also early Jain caves) |
| Ghantasala | Krishna | stupa and ancient port |
| Jaggayyapeta | Krishna valley | early relief sculpture |
| Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram | near Visakhapatnam | hill-top monasteries |
| Ramatirtham | Vizianagaram | Buddhist and Jain remains |

**Terms explained**
- **Hinayana / Mahayana / Vajrayana** — the three historical phases of Buddhism (older, 'great-vehicle', and tantric).
- **Bhattiprolu script** — an early southern form of Brahmi found on the Bhattiprolu caskets.
- **Chaitya** — a rock-cut or built Buddhist prayer hall.

**Don't confuse**
- **Bhattiprolu** (Guntur/Krishna) is NOT **Salihundam** (Srikakulam/Vamsadhara) — different districts and rivers.
- The Visakhapatnam hill trio is **Thotlakonda, Bavikonda and Sankaram**, not the Krishna-valley stupas.

**Remember it:** 'Bhattiprolu = early Brahmi caskets; Salihundam = Srikakulam, Vamsadhara, all three phases; Vizag hills = Thotlakonda + Bavikonda + Sankaram'.

**TL;DR**
- Andhra has one of India's densest clusters of ancient Buddhist sites.
- Krishna-valley core: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli.
- Visakhapatnam hill monasteries: Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram.
- Bhattiprolu = early southern Brahmi script; Salihundam (Srikakulam, Vamsadhara) = all three Buddhist phases.
keyPoints: Andhra has one of India's densest clusters of ancient Buddhist sites.
Krishna-valley core: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli.
Visakhapatnam hill monasteries: Thotlakonda, Bavikonda, Sankaram (Bojjannakonda).
Bhattiprolu relic caskets = early southern Brahmi (Bhattiprolu script), ancestor of Telugu-Kannada.
Salihundam (Srikakulam, Vamsadhara) shows Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana phases.

items.title: Salankayanas & Vishnukundins — the Vengi Successors
items.body:
## From the Ikshvakus to the Eastern Chalukyas

**In one line:** After the Ikshvakus, two dynasties — the Salankayanas and then the Vishnukundins — held coastal Andhra from Vengi, until the Chalukyas took over and founded the Eastern Chalukya line.

**The story**
The political centre of coastal Andhra now shifted to **Vengi**. First came the **Salankayanas (c. 300–440 CE)**, who ruled the **Godavari–Krishna doab** (the land between the two rivers) from **Vengi (Pedavegi, near Eluru)**. They used the **bull (Nandi)** as their emblem — the source of their name — and began as feudatories of the Pallavas before standing on their own. Next, the **Vishnukundins (5th–7th centuries CE)** **took coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas**; their greatest king **Madhava Varma** performed **Vedic sacrifices including the ashvamedha**, and the dynasty is linked with capitals such as **Denduluru**. To their period belong the early rock-cut cave temples at **Undavalli** (with its huge reclining Vishnu), **Mogalrajapuram** and **Bhairavakonda** — a sign of Brahmanical architecture growing up beside the older Buddhist tradition. Finally, the Badami Chalukya emperor **Pulakeshin II** conquered the eastern Deccan and installed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**, who founded the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (from 624 CE)**.

**Why it is asked**
The succession chain and the 'Pulakeshin II → Kubja Vishnuvardhana → Eastern Chalukyas' hand-over are favourite ordering and cause-effect questions.

**Picture it**

```
Dhanyakataka (Satavahanas) → Vijayapuri (Ikshvakus) → Vengi (Salankayanas → Vishnukundins) → Eastern Chalukyas
```

| Dynasty | Period | Capital | Marker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salankayanas | c. 300–440 CE | Vengi (Pedavegi) | bull (Nandi) emblem |
| Vishnukundins | 5th–7th c CE | Denduluru (etc.) | Madhava Varma; ashvamedha |
| Eastern Chalukyas | from 624 CE | Vengi | founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana |

**Terms explained**
- **Doab** — the fertile land between two rivers (here the Godavari and the Krishna).
- **Vengi** — the long-lasting political nucleus of coastal Andhra (identified with Pedavegi).
- **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** — brother of Pulakeshin II; founder of the Eastern Chalukyas.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Salankayanas** (bull emblem, Vengi) ruled BEFORE the **Vishnukundins** (Madhava Varma) — keep the order.
- The Vishnukundins were ended by the **Chalukyas (Pulakeshin II)**, NOT by the Pallavas, Ikshvakus or Satavahanas.

**Remember it:** 'Vengi line — Salankayanas (bull) → Vishnukundins (Madhava Varma) → Pulakeshin II hands it to the Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE)'.

**TL;DR**
- Salankayanas (c. 300–440 CE) ruled the Godavari–Krishna doab from Vengi (Pedavegi); bull emblem.
- Vishnukundins (5th–7th c CE) took coastal Andhra; greatest king Madhava Varma (ashvamedha); Undavalli/Mogalrajapuram/Bhairavakonda caves.
- Pulakeshin II ended them; Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (624 CE).
- Political centre steadily shifted: Dhanyakataka → Vijayapuri → Vengi → Eastern Chalukyas.
keyPoints: Salankayanas (c.300-440 CE) ruled the Godavari-Krishna doab from Vengi (Pedavegi); bull emblem.
Vishnukundins (5th-7th c CE) took coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas; greatest king Madhava Varma (ashvamedha).
Vishnukundin rule ended by Chalukya Pulakeshin II, who installed Kubja Vishnuvardhana -> Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE).
Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda cave temples belong to the Vishnukundi period.
Political centre shifted: Dhanyakataka -> Vijayapuri -> Vengi -> Eastern Chalukyas.
items.source: Wikipedia — Salankayana / Vishnukundina dynasties; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi) — verified

items.title: For Mains — Ancient Andhra (Satavahanas to Vishnukundins)
items.body:
## For Mains — ancient Andhra as a theme

Mains Paper-II (clause **M2-6**: AP Ancient — Satavahanas, Ikshvakus, Salankayanas, Pallavas, Vishnukundins, Eastern Chalukyas, Renati Cholas) wants a synthesis, not a king-list. The strongest thesis: **ancient Andhra was a Buddhist and maritime heartland that gradually 'Brahmanised', with Vengi emerging as its lasting political nucleus.** Argue along dimensions.

**Dimensions the question can take**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political succession | Satavahanas (Dhanyakataka) → Ikshvakus (Vijayapuri) → Salankayanas and Vishnukundins (Vengi) → Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE) |
| Religion | Buddhist zenith under Satavahanas/Ikshvakus; the Vedic-king / Buddhist-queen split; shift to Brahmanical temples under the Vishnukundins |
| Art & architecture | Amaravati school (white limestone, ayaka pillars) → rock-cut caves at Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram, Bhairavakonda; Gudimallam early Siva-linga |
| Economy | Krishna–Godavari delta surplus; Indo-Roman trade via Ghantasala and coastal ports |
| Language & thought | Prakrit (Bhattiprolu Brahmi) edging toward Telugu; Nagarjuna's Madhyamika philosophy; Gunadhya's Brihatkatha |
| Legacy | Vengi as the enduring centre; seed-bed of Telugu culture under the Eastern Chalukyas |

**Data points / sources to quote**
- **Amaravati & Nagarjunakonda** — the Buddhist art zenith; ayaka pillars; Sri Lankan monks' vihara.
- **Bhattiprolu caskets** — earliest southern Brahmi, ancestor of the Telugu script.
- **Acharya Nagarjuna** — Madhyamika/Sunyavada, Mula-madhyamaka-karika.
- **Nasik Prashasti / Dhanyakataka** — the Satavahana imperial and religious footprint in Andhra.
- **Pulakeshin II's Aihole-era conquest** — the 624 CE transition to the Eastern Chalukyas.

**AP angle (central here)**
This entire subtopic IS the AP angle — it is the foundation chapter of Andhra's own history. Stress Amaravati (also the modern capital's namesake), the submerged-and-saved Nagarjunakonda, and the unbroken thread to Telugu literature.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the thesis: 'Ancient Andhra evolved from a Buddhist-maritime heartland into a Brahmanical polity centred on Vengi.'
- Use the succession arrow (Dhanyakataka → Vijayapuri → Vengi) as a one-line spine.
- Diagram idea: a timeline band with a religion axis above (Buddhism fading, temples rising) and a political axis below (the shifting capitals).
- Close on legacy: Vengi and the Eastern Chalukyas carried this heritage into the age of written Telugu.
keyPoints: Thesis: ancient Andhra moved from a Buddhist-maritime heartland to a Brahmanical polity centred on Vengi.
Succession spine: Dhanyakataka (Satavahanas) → Vijayapuri (Ikshvakus) → Vengi (Salankayanas, Vishnukundins) → Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE).
Religion: Buddhist zenith (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda), Vedic-king/Buddhist-queen split, then temple-building.
Art: Amaravati school and ayaka pillars → rock-cut caves (Undavalli); Gudimallam early Siva-linga.
Thought & language: Nagarjuna's Madhyamika; Bhattiprolu Brahmi edging toward Telugu.
AP angle is central: foundation chapter of Andhra history and Telugu culture.
items.source: History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi); Wikipedia (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Salankayana, Vishnukundina, Eastern Chalukyas) — as of Oct 2026
